The polytheists of Arabia found the reality of the Hereafter extremely difficult to grasp. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) presented this reality to them, they reacted with intense psychological resistance. They regarded it as astonishing, strange, and a frightening kind of belief. For this reason they rejected it with great vehemence, and in various ways they challenged the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to bring about that Day. At times they said, "At least tell us its appointed time."

In a report related from Hadrat Ibn Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him), it is mentioned that the person who asked about the punishment of the Day of Resurrection was Nadr ibn al-Harith. In another narration, the question came from the disbelievers, who said, "Bring the punishment," and Allah said that there was no need to ask for it, for it would surely come upon the disbelievers.

In any case, there was someone who made the demand, "Let the Resurrection come and let the punishment befall them." So Allah said that it is coming very soon, for Allah has decreed it. You consider it distant, but it is near, and no one can avert it or hold it back. Therefore, to demand it when it is certain to occur is nothing but the misfortune of the one who asks, whether the questioner was one person or many. In any case, the question was asked.

The disbelievers are absolutely deserving of punishment, whether they ask about the Resurrection or not, and this punishment is certain to occur. It comes from Allah, the Lord of the ascending stairways, who is worthy of every kind of exaltedness, who is of lofty ranks, and who is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.

After this opening statement, in which a decisive word was given on the subject of punishment, namely that it will occur, that such-and-such people will be its recipients, and that it will come from Allah, who is exalted and possessed of power, and that His decree concerning it is binding and no power can repel it, the details of that Day of Punishment, about which these people are hurrying, now come into view. It is near, but the reckoning of time with Allah is very different from the reckoning of time among human beings. There is a great difference between Allah's measures and human measures; the standard of Allah and the standard of man are different.

The angels and the Spirit ascend to Him in a Day, the measure of which is fifty thousand years. So be patient, with graceful patience. They see it as distant, but We see it as near. (70:4–7)

The sound view is that the Day referred to is the Day of Judgement, because the context does not specify any other meaning. On that day the angels and the Spirit ascend to Allah, and the Spirit, according to the more reliable narration, is Jibril (ʿAlayhi al-Salam), as he is named by this name in other places. The mention of the angels followed by the specific mention of the Spirit indicates a high station, and in connection with that Day it shows that the angels and Ruh al-Amin will ascend on that Day. This indicates that it will be a very important Day, and that it will have this distinctive quality. On that Day they will ascend regarding its arrangements and affairs. We do not know, nor has Allah made us responsible for knowing, what affairs their hurrying will be for, nor how these angels will ascend, nor where they will go upon ascending. These are matters of the unseen (ghayb), and the meaning of this verse will not be increased by them. Nor do we have any proof for them. It is only that it will be a very important Day, in which such important beings will be exceedingly occupied.

As for this expression:

"Its measure is fifty thousand years" (70:4), it may refer to a long period of time, and this usage is common in Arabic idiom. It may also refer to a definite period, or it may be that in reality it is a long day of fifty thousand years in the manner of the years of this world. In our age this reality has become easier to grasp, because our day is formed by the axial rotation of the earth, which is completed in twenty-four hours, and there are also stars whose axial rotation takes many thousands of times longer than the rotation of our star, the earth. This does not mean that seventy thousand or fifty thousand years is a specific period of time; rather it refers to a standard, one of the standards of Allah.

And if one of the days of Allah is equal to fifty thousand years, then the punishment of the Day of Judgement, which these people see as far off, is near in the sight of Allah. This is why the Prophet (ﷺ) is told to bear with beautiful patience and not to be distressed by their denial and their hastening regarding the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verse 5:

﴿So be patient with a becoming patience.﴾ ﴿They see it as far off, but We see it as near.﴾ (70:5-7)

The call to patience has been addressed to every caller (da'i) to the truth. Every Messenger was given this same guidance to be patient, and the believing followers of the Messengers were also commanded to observe "sabr jamil" (beautiful patience). The importance of this is evident, since the path is so arduous and the call so heavy, and the weak human soul needs so much protection against slips. The goal of the Islamic revolution appears distant, and its aim and destination lie far off on the horizon and at a great height.

By "sabr jamil" is meant that patience with which the one who is patient is at peace; during it, the one who is patient feels no distress, restlessness or doubt. He should be certain that the promise made to him is true. The state of the one who is patient should be that his end will be better, that he is content with the decree of Allah, and that, regarding the trial that is coming, he believes that divine wisdom lies within it. The one who is patient should also understand that whatever calamity befalls him comes from Allah, and that he will be given its reward.

This is the patience that has been called "sabr jamil", and it is this patience that befits a caller (da'i), because he calls to Allah and invites to the call of Allah. In it he has nothing of his own; his personal interests are not tied to this call. Therefore, the afflictions upon him are in the way of Allah, and the decisions made about him are the decisions of Allah. Hence, "sabr jamil" is that which is realistic and becoming, and the one who is patient should have a deep awareness of these matters.

This call, against which the deniers stand up and obstruct its path, is the call of Allah, and the Resurrection, which they deny and for whose arrival they demand haste, is also part of His call. It is He who, according to His plan and wisdom, determines the time of its establishment. But people fail to grasp this plan and decree, and they demand haste. When much time passes, they begin to doubt it. Sometimes the caller himself feels intense restlessness, and desire arises in their hearts that Allah's promise come to pass quickly; it is in such moments that the caller is given this guidance.

﴿So be patient, a becoming patience.﴾ (70:8 for the continuation, cf. 70:5-7)

Here the address is to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so that his blessed heart may bear the pain of opposition and denial. And together with this, he should understand another reality: the measures of events and affairs with Allah are different from those with people.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verses 6–7:

"They see it as far away, but We see it as near" (70:6–7). After this, scenes of that Day are presented, the Day on which the promised punishment will come, which they consider distant while Allah considers it near. These scenes occur in this universe and also within the psychological world of man. They will be so terrifying that human faculties will be bewildered, and an earthquake will take place within the universe and within the human soul.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verses 8–9:

"On the Day when the sky will be like molten silver, and the mountains will become like tufts of wool." (70:8–9)

Muhl (مہل) means raw minerals being melted, such as the dregs of oil. Al-ihn (العهن) means a dyed woolen cloth.

The Qur'an informs us in various places that great events will take place on that Day. Because of them, the present condition of the celestial bodies of this world will not remain. Their qualities, circumstances and form will change, and among them this sky will become like molten minerals. Those who research the physical sciences should reflect on these verses. According to them, it is an established fact that all celestial bodies were originally solidified from molten matter, to the extent that this matter was in the form of gas, and the state of gas comes after the state of melting and becoming fluid. Perhaps all this matter will be extinguished on the Day of Resurrection, as it has been said:

"And when the stars fall dark." (81:2)

And, cooling down and becoming fluid, their gaseous nature will thus change.

However, this is only a possibility, and those who investigate from this angle may find interest in it. As far as we are concerned, we believe in the meaning of the verse, in which a frightening picture is drawn: the sky will be like molten material, and the mountains will be like carded, multicolored wool. It will be a most dreadful scene, which the Qur'an describes in these terrifying words.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verses 10–14:

"And no close friend will ask after a close friend, though they will be made to see one another. The guilty one would wish to ransom himself from the punishment of that Day with his children, his wife, his brother, his family that sheltered him, and all who are on earth, and then that this might deliver him."

On that Day people will be extremely distressed, and each will be preoccupied with himself. No one will find the opportunity to turn toward anyone other than himself, and there will be no room in his consciousness for anyone else. Even a close friend will not ask after a close friend. There will be a fear that numbs the senses, and because of it all ties between people will be severed, and every person will be enveloped in his own problems and his own anguish. They will be presented to one another and made to see one another, and this will be done deliberately, yet each will be concerned only with himself. Every conscience will have its own preoccupation. Therefore a friend will not ask after a friend, and no one will be able to seek help from another.

And what will be the state of the guilty one? His soul will be in the grip of fear. His very sense of feeling will be gone, and to save himself from the punishment of that Day he will be ready to give up his most precious possession, which in this life he clung to, and for which his whole life was lived: such as his children, his wife, his brother, and his family, who are supporters and helpers. Indeed, on that Day, to save his own soul he will be ready to give up all the wealth and power of this entire world, so that somehow he may be saved. How dreadful a picture of anguish and sorrow this is. This person is half-senseless, and is ready to give up the whole universe. This manner of expression is peculiar to the Qur'an.

This is the condition of the guilty one, and these are his wishes. In that state he sees such circumstances that the last spark of hope is extinguished, false desires come to an end, and the true and real state of affairs comes before him.

Translation of the passage:

"No indeed! It is a blazing flame, stripping away the flesh from the head and skin, calling out to everyone who turned his back and withdrew, and gathered wealth and hoarded it." This is a scene which, upon seeing it, makes a man's fourteen layers (of senses) light up, whereas before this scene he was in a stupor because of grief and sorrow. Kalla (کلا) is a word of most stern rejection and rebuke. Such a thing can never happen. These are false wishes: that someone could ransom himself with his sons, wife, husband, brother, sister, family, and all the property of the earth. No indeed.

"Inaha la-zā" (07:61): "It is a blazing flame."

"Nazzā'atan lish-shawā" (07:61): "Stripping away the flesh." It strips the flesh of the face and the head, and then it will appear in the form of a monstrous being, moving alive. And in this terror, it will deliberately be increasing its own fury.

Translation of the passage:

This is a scene which, upon seeing it, makes a man's fourteen layers (of senses) light up, whereas before this scene he was in a stupor because of grief and sorrow. These are false wishes: that someone could ransom himself with his sons, wife, husband, brother, sister, family, and all the property of the earth. No indeed.

"Inaha la-zā" (07:61): "It is a blazing flame."

"Nazzā'atan lish-shawā" (07:61): "Stripping away the flesh." It strips the flesh of the face and the head, and then it will appear in the form of a monstrous being, moving alive. And in this terror, it will deliberately be increasing its own fury.

﴿Calling out, it will summon everyone who turned away and withdrew, and who amassed wealth and hoarded it.﴾ (07 : 81)

This Fire will call to those who turned away from the truth and withdrew from it, just as they were called to the path of guidance in the world before. In the world they would turn their backs and walk away. Today, however, when the Fire calls them, they are not in a position to turn their backs and leave. Before this, they were busy amassing wealth against the Islamic call, and they kept that wealth stored in vessels and treasure chests. Today, the call comes from the Fire of Jahannam. It cannot be rejected, and no one can ransom himself from it with wealth.

In this Surah, in the Surah before it, and in Surah al-Qalam, emphasis is placed on the fact that their crimes included this: they amassed wealth and did not urge people to feed the needy. So, alongside disbelief, polytheism and denial, this was also their crime. This shows that, alongside disbelief, misguidance and denial, the movement in Makkah also faced the difficulty that people were stingy and worshippers of wealth, and they did not care for the poor. Therefore, again and again, attention was drawn to these matters too: neglecting the poor and the needy, and being excessively devoted to wealth and materialism, brings punishment.

This Surah also contains other indications which show what the features of the Makkan society were in which the Islamic call began. It was a society in which people were engaged in gathering wealth and property. Trade and usury had spread everywhere. The chieftains of Quraysh owned trading houses, and each had his own caravans, which travelled in summer and winter. People pounced upon wealth from every side. Every individual was extremely stingy. The poor and the needy were deprived. Orphans and the helpless went hungry. For this reason, the Qur'an repeatedly issued commands and repeatedly condemned greed in order to remove this economic imbalance. It entered into human souls and uprooted stinginess and greed. Islam did this first on the level of ideas before the conquest, and after the conquest it did it in practice. For example, riba (usury) was prohibited. People were forbidden to consume the wealth of others by false means. Consuming the property of orphans was described as eating fire, and extravagance and oppression in dealing with orphans' property were forbidden. Marriage with orphans was forbidden as a means of keeping their property in one's hands, and the desire to marry orphan girls merely in order to seize their wealth was condemned. In short, the measures, guidance and warnings given show what the economic condition of the people was at that time, and what the eternal economic policy of Islam is. For any Islamic society, the lasting guidance is this: beware of stinginess, envy and greed, free yourselves from materialism and the chains of wealth. This policy has been maintained throughout the Qur'an.

Earlier, the terrifying scenes of the Day of Judgement were shown, in the form of fear and punishment. Now it is explained how the human soul reacts on different occasions of joy and sorrow. It is explained how a person reacts to different circumstances in the state of faith, and it is also explained what the reaction is in the state of faith. And what happens in the absence of faith. It is explained what the end of the believers is, and what the end of the disbelievers is.

For this reason, the Qur'an repeatedly issued commands and repeatedly condemned greed in order to remove this economic imbalance. It entered into human souls and uprooted stinginess and greed. Islam did this first on the level of ideas before the conquest, and after the conquest it did it in practice. For example, riba (usury) was prohibited. People were forbidden to consume the wealth of others by false means. Consuming the property of orphans was described as eating fire, and extravagance and oppression in dealing with orphans' property were forbidden. Marriage with orphans was forbidden as a means of keeping their property in one's hands, and the desire to marry orphan girls merely in order to seize their wealth was condemned. In short, the measures, guidance and warnings given show what the economic condition of the people was at that time, and what the eternal economic policy of Islam is. For any Islamic society, the lasting guidance is this: beware of stinginess, envy and greed, free yourselves from materialism and the chains of wealth. This policy has been maintained throughout the Qur'an.

Earlier, the terrifying scenes of the Day of Judgement were shown, in the form of fear and punishment. Now it is explained how the human soul reacts on different occasions of joy and sorrow. It is explained how a person reacts to different circumstances in the state of faith, and it is also explained what the reaction is in the state of faith. And what happens in the absence of faith. It is explained what the end of the believers is, and what the end of the disbelievers is.

This is the human being without faith. Look closely at this portrait: the Qur'an draws the picture of such a person with great truthfulness, and the features of a non-believing person stand out clearly in it. A person is protected from all these features only when he is a believer. When a believer is struck by a calamity, he is a picture of *sabr jamil* (beautiful patience) and remains composed, far from *jaza' wa faza'* (anguished wailing and lamentation). And if he is granted prosperity, he neither becomes miserly nor boasts.

﴿Indeed, mankind was created anxious. When evil touches him, he is distressed; and when good touches him, he is withholding.﴾ (70:19–21)

"Indeed, mankind was created in a state of distress and is anxious when hardship comes upon him, and when prosperity is granted to him, he becomes miserly." In this way, each word appears as a stroke of the Divine Artist, and it clearly describes the human face and its characteristics. When a person reads these very brief three verses and sees that only a few words have been used in them, he sees a remarkably vivid and clear portrait of a human being devoid of faith. All its features are prominent. *Hal'* (anxiety), *jaza'* (impatience) and *mana'* (withholding): when any calamity befalls this person, or some sting of the realities of life touches him, he begins to lament. He thinks that he will remain in this condition forever. He thinks that he is now trapped in this calamity permanently, and that there is no one who can rescue him from it. He begins to feel as though this moment of calamity is everlasting. At such a time, this person becomes bound by illusions, and his calamity and hardship increase. It does not even occur to him that ease may come after this difficulty. He does not hope for any mercy or kindness from Allah. Thus this lamentation consumes him, and his personality becomes shattered. The real cause of this condition is that he is not under the protection of a Mighty Being, and he has no firm support in which he places any hope.

On the other hand, if he is prosperous and in comfort, he is one who refrains from doing any good deed. He thinks that these comforts have been obtained by him through his own effort and toil, so he reserves them for himself, hides them for his own self, and in fact becomes a slave to his possessions, ready to lay down his life for his property and wealth. This is because he does not know what the reality of provision is, and what the role of the human being himself is in receiving provision. This person does not hope that, [whether] in either condition, [he is] sustained: in the state of good and also in the state of evil. This is a very evil portrait of a human being, but of a human being whose heart is empty of the light of faith.

Therefore, believing in Allah is in reality a very important matter. It is not merely a word that is uttered with the tongue, nor does it relate only to a few religious rituals and acts of worship. It is in reality a psychological state, a complete system of life, and a standard for events and circumstances. When a person's heart becomes empty of faith, he becomes so light, like a single feather of a bird that the gusts of wind blow here and there, carrying it about; it has no weight and no measure. This kind of person always remains a victim of anxiety and fear. If he is struck by some calamity, he laments; if some good comes to him, he becomes stingy. But if his vessel is filled with faith, he remains in complete tranquility and well-being, because his connection is with a real source from which all events and circumstances are controlled. He is content with Allah's decree, whether it be good or evil. If it is good, he is content; he is conscious of Allah's mercy. In Allah's trials, he always keeps the lamp of hope burning, knowing that after difficulty comes ease. He hopes that after every difficulty there comes ease. If he receives good, he knows that he has certain obligations; he spends for them, and he will receive his reward in the Hereafter. Indeed, he will be rewarded in both this world and the Hereafter. Therefore, faith is in this world a kind of earnings whose reward is received in the Hereafter, and because of it a person attains comfort, tranquility and stability. And throughout his life he remains in this state. The people of faith are exempted from this condition.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 70, verse 22:

Then what are their qualities? From those general human qualities mentioned above, a believer is exempted. For example:

﴿Except those who observe prayer (al-musallin)﴾ (22) ﴿Those who are constant in their prayer﴾ (32) (70:22 to 32) "Except those who are steadfast in prayer, who are constant in observing their prayer."

Prayer (salah) is fundamentally a pillar of Islam and a sign of faith, but its wisdom is that it is in reality a means of connection with Allah. It is a manifestation of a relationship in which only the servant and his Lord stand face to face. The servant is at the lofty station of servanthood, and the Lord, exalted is He, is at the lofty station of lordship and deity. It has been said about this that the enduring quality of faith is constancy in prayer.

Those who are constant in their prayers (70:23). Constancy and continuity in prayer is an essential attribute. A prayer performed as a mere formality, or performed carelessly, is not a complete prayer. Laziness and negligence regarding prayer are reprehensible. Since prayer is the connection between the servant and the Lord, constancy in it is indispensable. When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) undertook any act of worship, he would adhere to it constantly. In a noble hadith it is stated: "The most beloved of deeds to Allah is that which is done consistently, even if it is little." Therefore, this sacred connection with Allah should be lasting. It should not be subject to whim, such that it is done sometimes and not at other times, as one pleases.

Those in whose wealth there is a known right (ḥaqq maʿlūm) for the beggar and the deprived (al-maḥrūm), (70:24–25)

The Qur'anic quotation is: ﴿Those in whose wealth there is a known right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ (70:24–25).

That is, the prescribed charities that are known and specified are the right of the poor in the wealth of the believers. The more comprehensive meaning of "a known right" is that they themselves set aside a specific portion of their wealth for the needy, and they say of their own accord that this is their right. In this way they overcome the impulse of miserliness and stinginess. Likewise, the awareness arises that members of society have responsibilities toward the destitute; the Islamic ummah in particular is a mutually supportive community.

The beggar (sāʾil) is one who asks, while the deprived (maḥrūm) is the destitute person who does not ask and does not express his need before anyone, and thus remains deprived. Alternatively, the deprived is the person upon whom some calamity has fallen, who has been deprived of blessings, and who has refrained from asking.

The awareness that the needy and deprived also have a share in wealth is, on one hand, an awareness of Allah's bounty, and on the other, an awareness of human brotherhood. Psychologically, the benefit is that a person is freed from the bonds of miserliness and stinginess, and there is also a collective guarantee in this. Therefore, there are many benefits in fulfilling the financial rights of society. In short, zakat and charity have psychological, personal and social benefits. Here, its mention is in relation to the psychological cure of a human being.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verse 26:

﴿Those who believe in the Day of Judgment (al-Din)﴾ (70:26). This quality is directly related to the central theme of this surah, since the surah's core subject is the Resurrection. Here, however, the passage discusses the psychological state of a believer. Belief in the Resurrection is an important part of the articles of faith (iman), and it has both a conscious and a practical effect on the shaping of a way of life. The one who affirms the Resurrection has values and measures that are different, and the one who does not affirm it is in doubt about it, and his values are entirely distinct, whether they relate to ideas, actions, or the important events of life.

The one who believes in the Resurrection acts in accordance with the balance and system of the heavens (God). He prepares for the reckoning of the Hereafter. He does not focus his gaze only on this world. And when he encounters events and circumstances in life, whether good or bad, his reaction is that these are the temporary conditions of this world, and the true abode is elsewhere. Therefore he corrects his Resurrection (his final end), whereas the one who denies the Hereafter has everything devoted to this world alone.

If he loses something here, then in his view he has lost everything, because all his activities are for this world. Thus his standards of reckoning are different, and he reaches a mistaken conclusion in every matter. He confines himself within the brief time of this limited world. Thus this wretched, wretched and miserable person is always afflicted with torment and caught in anguish, because all his estimates about this world are wrong. He is never content or happy, and he never makes just and equitable decisions, because his decisions are confined within the limited circle of this world. Therefore he himself is troubled and also troubles his environment. "A heart in distress, a rope tangled..." In short, even in this world he does not find a life based on high values. This is the reason why, in Islam, belief in the Last Day has been made a part of the Islamic worldview.

Those who fear the punishment of their Lord, for the punishment of their Lord is not a thing from which anyone may feel secure (70:27-28; 7:72-82). This is a stage beyond mere affirmation of the Hereafter. It is greater sensitivity regarding the Last Day, a fresh awareness of Allah's watchfulness, a consciousness of shortcoming before Allah's court, and greater devotion in worship. It is the fear that Allah's punishment may come at any moment. Therefore, such people are always conscious of the wrath of Allah, and they continually seek Allah's protection and refuge.

The Prophet ﷺ used to fear the punishment of Allah, although his station with Allah was well known, and he himself knew well that he was chosen and that Allah's favours were upon him. He was certain that only Allah's grace could admit him into Paradise. Therefore he said to his Companions: "No one's deeds will ever admit him into Paradise." The Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) asked: "O Messenger of Allah, not even you?" He said: "Not even I, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." (Bukhari and Muslim)

Indeed, the punishment of their Lord is not something against which one may feel secure. (Qur'an 70:28)

This indicates that one should always fear the punishment of Allah and never be heedless of it even for a moment. At times, actions that bring about punishment are committed during moments of heedlessness; therefore, heedlessness is extremely dangerous. Allah's purpose is that people remain alert and awake at all times. Yet, even if weakness has occurred from them despite this, Allah's mercy is vast, His forgiveness is ready, and the door of repentance is open; it is not closed. This is the balanced position of Islam, which lies between heedlessness and excessive anxiety: a person's heart should remain connected to Allah, he should fear Him, hope for His mercy, and also remain content in His mercy.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verses 29–30:

Those who guard their private parts, except from their wives or those whom their right hands possess, for in that case they are not blameworthy; but whoever seeks beyond that, it is they who are the transgressors. (Qur'an 70:29–31, cited here as 7:92–13 in the source's reference)

Therefore they may enter into a pure relationship with their wives and with the slave women they possess, and this relationship should be both pure and lawful. Islam prescribes the only lawful path to having slave women in the following manner: women who come as prisoners of war, where the Islamic government has not decided to release them by ransom or as a favour. In this regard, the following verse of Surah Muhammad lays down the principle:

"So when you meet those who disbelieve in battle, then strike the necks until, when you have inflicted slaughter upon them, then secure their bonds, and afterwards either release them as a favour or ransom them, until the war lays down its burdens." (Qur'an 47:4)

However, at times a prisoner is neither exchanged, nor is a ransom obtained, and the Islamic government does not intend to release them as a favour. In such a case, the male or female prisoners will be slaves, for as long as the opposing side enslaves Muslim prisoners, even if the enemy nation gives slavery some other name. Thus, in this unavoidable situation, Islam has permitted only their owners to have relations with the slave women, and Islam has then arranged for the freedom of these slaves through one of the means it prescribed for their emancipation. The Qur'an arranged for the freedom of slaves through several means. In this way Islam made a clear arrangement for absorbing captive women into society, so that they would not roam about in the community like unrestrained animals spreading corruption; thus they would not be left free in society to do as they please.

﴿Fa man ... al-ʿādūn﴾ (08 : 13) "But whoever seeks beyond that, they are the transgressors." Thus Islam places a barrier against every kind of sexual filth. Apart from these two clear permissible forms, sexual relations are forbidden. Islam does not perceive any filth in the sexual relation itself, but it declares all relations outside these two lawful forms to be forbidden. Islam desires a clean, pure, clear and open social system.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on surah 70, verse 32:

﴿Those who are faithful to their trusts and to their covenants﴾ (23:07). These are the moral values on which Islam builds its society. The concept of safeguarding trusts and honouring covenants in society arises from the safeguarding and observance of the Great Trust, which Allah offered to the heavens, the earth and the mountains. They refused to bear it and feared it, for it is a very great and heavy burden, but man took it up. This was the trust of the Islamic way of life, the trust of the belief in the Oneness of Allah, and man accepted it by choice, not by compulsion. This is the trust that humanity accepted when they were in the loins of their fathers, and they were made witnesses to it, and their very creation bears witness to it. From this trust and faithfulness it follows that one must fulfil all covenants in the world. Accordingly, Islam has dealt very strictly in the fulfilment of covenants, and its injunctions have been emphasised so that the Islamic society may be established upon very firm principles. Faithfulness, trustworthiness and the observance of covenants have been declared a distinguishing quality of the believing soul, while betrayal and breach of promise have been declared a quality of the disbelievers. The Qur'an has repeated this again and again and emphasised it, so that there should be no doubt that trustworthiness and fidelity to covenants are among the fundamental aims of Islam.

"Those who stand firm in their testimonies" (70:33). Allah has attached countless rights to the discharge of testimony. Indeed, the establishment of Allah's limits (hudud) depends upon testimony; if testimony is not upheld, the hudud cannot be established. Therefore, one should not commit the sin of withholding testimony, and when testimony is sought from someone, he should never conceal it. And testimony should be rendered correctly, without introducing irrelevant matters. Allah has described this testimony as the testimony of that person so that it may be connected with obedience to Allah. Elsewhere it is said:

﴿And establish testimony for Allah﴾ (65:2). And here He has counted it among the attributes of the believers. And this testimony is also one of the trusts (amanat); it is mentioned here separately because it is a very important obligation.

The heading reads: "And the attributes of the believers begin with prayer and also end with prayer."

﴿And those who guard their prayers.﴾ (70:34) — the verse quoted here in the commentary is 70:34, the same as the heading, and the commentary's own reference to 70:43 is preserved in the text below.

Correction to my own rendering above: the commentary's quoted verse reads ﴿And those who guard their prayers﴾ (Qur'an 70:34), and it is cited with the reference (07:43) in the original text, which I have kept as written. The rest of the passage follows.

Among the attributes mentioned at the beginning of the description of the believers, it was stated that they maintain their prayer constantly (dawam). Here it is mentioned that they guard their prayer (muhafazah), meaning they safeguard the obligatory elements of prayer, its times, its sunnah practices, its form, and its spirit. Therefore they do not perform it carelessly or lazily, nor do they waste it by failing to recite it properly. The purpose of mentioning prayer both at the beginning and at the end is to show that prayer holds a very great significance in Islam. It is upon this that the attributes of the believers conclude.

Now their end is also described here, whereas the end of the other party was mentioned earlier.

*Ulā'ika ... mukramūn* (7:53): "They will dwell in the gardens of Paradise with honour." This very brief verse brings together both sensory pleasure and moral dignity in one place. They will be in gardens and they will be honoured. Thus they will enjoy both delight and dignity. And this will be their distinction because of their faith, certainty and righteousness.

Now, at the end, a scene of Islamic da'wah. This is a Meccan scene. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is standing and calling people to faith, reciting the Qur'an, while the polytheists come rushing toward him from every side:

﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, that they hasten toward you with outstretched necks, from the right and from the left, in separate groups?﴾

Muhti' (مهطع) refers to one who walks swiftly while stretching out his neck, as though a rope were put around his neck and he were being dragged along. ʿIzīn (عزين) is the plural of ʿizah, whose form and meaning are both equivalent to firqah (فئة), meaning group.

In this there is both a satire on their suspicious behaviour and a depiction of this posture and movement. They are being marvelled at, and they are asked what has happened to them. These people are not rushing toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to listen to his words or to take guidance from him. Rather, in a state of bewildered agitation, they run to find out what he is saying, and then they run back. Having gone back to their own places, they sit in their circles and think about what schemes they should devise against him.

Now, at the end, a scene of Islamic da'wah. This is a Meccan scene. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) is standing and calling people to faith, reciting the Qur'an, while the polytheists come rushing toward him from every side:

﴿So what is wrong with those who disbelieve, that they hasten toward you with outstretched necks, from the right and from the left, in separate groups?﴾

Muhti' (مهطع) refers to one who walks swiftly while stretching out his neck, as though a rope were put around his neck and he were being dragged along. ʿIzīn (عزين) is the plural of ʿizah, whose form and meaning are both equivalent to firqah (فئة), meaning group.

In this there is both a satire on their suspicious behaviour and a depiction of this posture and movement. They are being marvelled at, and they are asked what has happened to them. These people are not rushing toward the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to listen to his words or to take guidance from him. Rather, in a state of bewildered agitation, they run to find out what he is saying, and then they run back. Having gone back to their own places, they sit in their circles and think about what schemes they should devise against him.

"Does every one of them hope to enter the Garden of Bliss? By no means! Indeed, We created them from what they know..." Wait, the passage given is the Urdu commentary on verse 38, so I translate it as it stands.

Here is the translation:

"And even in their present state they would be among the people of Paradise? Nay, such criminals will be enveloped in the Fire. Perhaps people consider themselves something great in the sight of Allah. Therefore they commit disbelief. They also cause pain to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). They listen to the Qur'an and then plot in secret, and yet they still expect to enter the Garden of Bliss, because they consider themselves something great in the sight of Allah."

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verse 39:

"Kalla, inna khalaqnahum mimma ya'lamun..." (Surah al-Ma'arij 70:39)

That is, it is absolutely impossible. Their wish and their self-deception are rejected with the utmost contempt. They know that We created them from a worthless drop of water. The Qur'an makes them aware of their true reality. Thus the pride, arrogance and haughtiness that were within them are crushed to dust, and the edifice of their conceit collapses to the ground. And this is done by a single word, a mere indication that they know what We created them from. It is the best picture of human weakness, frailty and worthlessness. It is surprising that they have fallen into this misunderstanding, when their deeds are such. Then they consider themselves something great. They should look at the stages of their creation. Their importance before Allah, because of this disbelief of theirs, is not even equal to that of a mosquito. They are destined to be wrapped in the fire of Hell because of their disbelief. How can they expect the blessings of Allah?

Regarding their matter as unimportant, diminishing their significance, and breaking the idols of their greatness, Allah announces His decision that if they do not accept guidance, Allah will bring into being a people better than them in their place. They cannot frustrate Allah, and they will reach the very end they deserve.

Why swear an oath over this matter? The Lord of the Easts and the Wests is pointed to, and through Him the greatness of Allah is conveyed. By "the easts and the wests," the places where the stars rise may be meant, and these are very numerous in this vast and wide universe. It may also be understood to mean the easts that continually occur in different regions, these easts being present at every moment, because when the earth revolves on its axis, some place in the world is always east and some place is always west.

In any case, whatever the meaning of "the easts and the wests" may be, it conveys the immensity of this universe and gives rise to the idea of the greatness of the Creator of the universe. Is the affair of these worthless and valueless people, whom We created from that which they know, in need of an oath being sworn by the name of the Lord of the Easts and the Lord of the Wests? Whereas He is able to bring in their place other people like them, and they cannot overcome Him, cannot escape from Him, and cannot run away from Him anywhere.

When the discourse reaches this conclusion, and it is made clear how terrible the punishment of the Hereafter is, how great the humiliation of the disbelievers will be on that day, and how great the honour of the believers will be, the address turns again to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he should not be distressed and should leave these people to advance toward the punishment of that very day. At this point the scene of that punishment is described again here, and it is told how painful a scene it is.

Commentary of Sayyid Qutb (Fi Zilal al-Quran, Urdu translation) on Surah 70, verses 41–43:

﴿So leave them﴾ ... ﴿...they are promised.﴾

It is said to you that these are extremely worthless people, and that their end is extremely frightening. Thus the picture drawn of their state and wretchedness on the Day of Resurrection is, in itself, very frightening, while in this depiction and portrayal are colours of contempt and mockery. This is in response to the state in which these people, here in the world, considered themselves to be something great.

When these people come out of their graves, they will rush forward in such haste, in panic, as if they were running toward their shrines. The reference to the manner of their walking in the world is a mocking and derisive allusion. They used to rush to the shrines (astanas) at their fairs and festivals, and gather around those idols. These people are running quickly today as well, but there is a difference of heaven and earth between that stampede and this one.

Following this, their condition is portrayed:

﴿Their eyes will be lowered; humiliation will cover them.﴾ (70:44) By these words, the picture of their state is drawn vividly. They appear utterly exhausted and abased. Previously in the world their bustling, their laziness, and their play and frivolity were the case, but now they are humiliated and running about in every direction.

﴿This is the Day that they were promised.﴾ (70:44) They used to doubt it, deny it, and demand it hastily.

Thus the beginning and the end of the surah become one, and this circle of the question of resurrection after death also reaches its conclusion. And thus this struggle between the Jahili conception of life and the Islamic conception comes to its end.
